steps.title: Neural data as time series
steps.reflectionQuestion: What makes a neural recording different from a single voltage value?
steps.stepObjective: Recognize neural recordings as ordered voltage samples over time.
steps.explanation: BCI systems start with measurements over time. Learning to see samples as a time series makes spikes, noise, drift, and features easier to reason about.
steps.oneLineMaster: Keep measurements, units and timing together.

steps.title: Candidate event detection
steps.reflectionQuestion: How could a threshold mistake turn noise into fake spikes?
steps.stepObjective: Practice scanning a signal for threshold crossings that could represent spikes.
steps.explanation: A threshold rule turns a synthetic voltage trace into candidate events. The exercise separates numerical detection from evidence about a biological source.
steps.oneLineMaster: Count threshold episodes without claiming a biological source.

steps.title: Firing rate
steps.reflectionQuestion: What information does a mean event rate preserve, and what does it discard?
steps.stepObjective: Convert spike counts and time windows into a reusable firing-rate calculation.
steps.explanation: Firing rate compresses many spikes into a rate that can drive models and decoders. It is one of the cleanest bridges from biology to computation.
steps.oneLineMaster: Compare rates with their time windows and limitations.

steps.title: Signal noise
steps.reflectionQuestion: What evidence would convince you that an event is artifact instead of neural activity?
steps.stepObjective: Recognize possible artifact and describe evidence needed to investigate it.
steps.explanation: Noise is unwanted variation in the recording: movement artifact, electrical interference, cardiac contamination, electrode instability, or unrelated biological activity. Bad signal-to-noise makes a decoder learn the wrong thing.
steps.oneLineMaster: Investigate contamination before interpreting events.

steps.title: Filtering and smoothing
steps.reflectionQuestion: How could smoothing help an LFP feature but hurt spike timing?
steps.stepObjective: Calculate a moving average and explain its effect on peaks and boundaries.
steps.explanation: Filtering and smoothing are preprocessing steps. They reduce unwanted frequencies or local jumps, but every filter is a trade-off: clean enough to decode, not so aggressive that spikes, timing, or frequency-band evidence disappears.
steps.oneLineMaster: Describe what a filter changes and what it may discard.

steps.title: Feature extraction
steps.reflectionQuestion: Which feature would you try first for left vs. right cursor intent?
steps.stepObjective: Compute mean, RMS and a threshold count from a window and say what each one discards.
steps.explanation: Features are compact measurements, such as firing rate, band power, spike count, peak amplitude, or frequency content, that a decoder can use. Good features often matter more than a fancy model.
steps.oneLineMaster: Each feature keeps one property of a window; a decoder sees only what you kept.

steps.title: Population vectors & linear readouts
steps.reflectionQuestion: Why does combining evidence from many neurons give a more stable signal than any single neuron?
steps.stepObjective: Build a population vector from per-channel rates and explain why combining channels helps.
steps.explanation: Real BCIs rarely rely on one neuron. They combine activity across a population into a feature vector. This is the foundation of almost every modern decoder.
steps.oneLineMaster: A population readout combines many noisy channels so no single one decides.

steps.title: Simple decoder logic
steps.reflectionQuestion: What could make a simple left/right decoder reliable offline but weak in real use?
steps.stepObjective: Map extracted features to intent or action with a rule, threshold, or classifier.
steps.explanation: A decoder maps features to a command. A linear score with an explicit tie rule teaches the core idea behind more advanced decoders, and every output can be traced by hand.
steps.oneLineMaster: A decoder is a rule you can write down: score, boundary, tie rule.

steps.title: Calibration and decoder drift
steps.checkpointPrompt: Checkpoint A: What can cause a decoder to drift? How would you detect it? What would you recalibrate first?
steps.reflectionQuestion: If baseline firing rates shift but tuning structure remains, what does that suggest?
steps.stepObjective: Explain common drift causes and choose a first recalibration move.
steps.explanation: Neural features shift across minutes, days, and sessions. Calibration keeps the decoder aligned with the user's current signal before teams assume hardware failure.
steps.oneLineMaster: Check whether drift is an offset, a gain change or a tuning change before choosing the fix.

steps.title: Weighted linear decoder
steps.reflectionQuestion: If you can see and change the weights, how would you fix a decoder that is biased toward one direction?
steps.stepObjective: Read weights as contributions, and keep training, validation and test data separate when choosing and reporting a decoder.
steps.explanation: A weighted linear decoder is a set of weights applied to features. You can inspect every weight and contribution, which makes it a good place to learn honest evaluation.
steps.oneLineMaster: A linear decoder is just a weighted sum of features followed by a decision rule.

steps.title: Cursor-control BCI
steps.reflectionQuestion: Why does screen feedback change how the user learns the decoder?
steps.stepObjective: Connect neural decoding to visible cursor movement and user feedback.
steps.explanation: Cursor control ties decoding to visible feedback. The user learns through the loop, so latency, calibration, and output feel all matter.
steps.oneLineMaster: Decoded velocity is clipped and integrated into position, and the person watching closes the loop.

steps.title: Latency, timing budgets & user adaptation
steps.reflectionQuestion: In your latency budget, which stage would you shorten first, and what would that cost elsewhere, for example noisier rates from a shorter window?
steps.stepObjective: Quantify the cost of latency and understand how users adapt their strategy when feedback is delayed.
steps.explanation: Real BCIs have hard timing budgets. Latency changes both the decoder's job and the user's motor strategy.
steps.oneLineMaster: Latency is a budget, and in a feedback loop stale information causes overshoot.

steps.title: Closed-loop feedback
steps.reflectionQuestion: Which is more dangerous in this case: a false positive or a missed event?
steps.stepObjective: Practice the safety trade-off between detection, action, and feedback.
steps.explanation: Closed-loop systems sense, decide, act, and update. In neurotechnology, feedback must be useful without becoming unsafe, noisy, or too automatic for the user to understand.
steps.oneLineMaster: Convert error rates into actions per day at the real base rate before trusting a closed-loop rule.

steps.title: Online adaptation & recalibration
steps.checkpointPrompt: Checkpoint C: Given drifting features, what is the smallest change that restores performance without full retraining?
steps.reflectionQuestion: When should you just shift the baseline versus re-learn the entire weight vector?
steps.stepObjective: Distinguish baseline offset correction from full model re-fit and choose the right first action.
steps.explanation: Neural signals drift. Good systems detect the drift and apply the cheapest fix that restores control (baseline, gain, or full recal).
steps.oneLineMaster: Fix offsets, then scales, and refit the weights only when the mapping itself has changed.

steps.title: Confidence, error handling & graceful degradation
steps.checkpointPrompt: Checkpoint D: When the decoder reports low confidence, what should the interface do instead of silently acting?
steps.reflectionQuestion: Which is worse for user trust: a wrong action or a clear 'I am uncertain, please confirm' state?
steps.stepObjective: Design simple confidence-aware behavior and graceful fallback when the neural evidence is weak.
steps.explanation: A good BCI never hides uncertainty. It slows down, asks for confirmation, or hands control back to the user.
steps.oneLineMaster: Let the decoder abstain on weak evidence, and tell the user when it stays unsure.

steps.title: Safety engineering in closed-loop systems
steps.reflectionQuestion: If a false positive triggers stimulation, what single safety rule would you add first?
steps.stepObjective: Apply asymmetric cost thinking and basic interlocks to closed-loop neurotechnology.
steps.explanation: When the output is physical (stimulation, movement, speech), the cost of false positives and false negatives is no longer symmetric.
steps.oneLineMaster: Price each error, choose the operating point by cost, and add layers that work even when the detector is wrong.

steps.title: Human-centered BCI UX
steps.checkpointPrompt: Checkpoint B: What makes a closed-loop BCI safe? What could go wrong with false positives? How should the user stay in control?
steps.reflectionQuestion: What should the interface reveal when calibration changes or confidence drops?
steps.stepObjective: Treat feedback, latency, fatigue, calibration transparency, and autonomy as part of the BCI system.
steps.explanation: A BCI user needs clear feedback, low latency, manageable fatigue, understandable calibration, and real control over device behavior. The interface is not decoration; it is part of the neural feedback loop.
steps.oneLineMaster: The interface is part of the control loop: show uncertainty, announce changes, keep a stop within reach.

steps.title: Brain data safety and ethics
steps.reflectionQuestion: What data would you refuse to collect unless the user clearly opted in?
steps.stepObjective: Apply privacy, consent, minimization, and mental-data safety to BCI design.
steps.explanation: BCI data can reveal sensitive information about attention, intent, and state. Privacy and consent belong in the design, not at the end.
steps.oneLineMaster: Collect what a stated purpose needs, ask for specific consent, and keep the rest off the device.

steps.title: Data architecture, privacy & regulatory reality
steps.reflectionQuestion: If raw neural data must leave the device for training, what minimum protections must be in place?
steps.stepObjective: Reason about on-device vs cloud trade-offs, consent versioning, and high-level regulatory expectations for neural data.
steps.explanation: Neural data is special category data. Architecture, consent, and re-identification risk must be designed in from the start.
steps.oneLineMaster: Decide what crosses each device boundary and treat software changes as controlled design changes.

steps.title: Unit 20 Capstone: full toy BCI integration & reflection
steps.checkpointPrompt: Final Reflection: Assemble everything you have built (viewer → detector → weighted decoder → cursor) and write one honest paragraph on what would still be required to make this system useful for a real person.
steps.reflectionQuestion: Write a one-page reflection. (1) Your pipeline in four lines, each with its input, output and unit. (2) Two failure modes you tested and one you did not. (3) The drift or noise mechanism most likely to break it first, and how you would detect it. (4) The one safety rule you would require before any output reaches a person. (5) The next step a real team would staff.
steps.stepObjective: Produce a documented end-to-end toy BCI pipeline and a clear-eyed reflection on its limitations versus real clinical systems.
steps.explanation: The capstone connects baseline correction, threshold counting, a weighted decoder and a cursor step, then asks you to state precisely what the toy still cannot do.
steps.oneLineMaster: A real BCI engineer can build the toy, explain why it is still a toy, and know exactly what the next real step would be.

simulations.title: Spike or Noise?
simulations.scenario: In a synthetic recording exercise, several microelectrode channels show large deflections roughly once per second. They align with an ECG reference.
simulations.signalDescription: Approximately 1 Hz deflections, aligned with ECG QRS complexes and visible on multiple channels.
simulations.decisionQuestion: What is the best next analytical step?

choices.label: Flag possible cardiac contamination and inspect synchronized raw traces
choices.rationale: ECG and cross-channel timing support investigation of contamination. Confirm the context before deciding which segments or methods are appropriate; threshold alone does not identify a neuron.

choices.label: Lower the spike threshold to catch more events
choices.rationale: Weaker — this would let in even more artifact. Threshold is not the underlying problem.

choices.label: Increase stimulation to mask the signal
choices.rationale: Unsafe — stimulation should not be used to mask recording artifacts; you'd inject current without clinical justification.

choices.label: Replace the electrode immediately
choices.rationale: This synthetic analysis does not justify a hardware or patient intervention. Investigate the recording evidence first.

simulations.oneLineMaster: ECG alignment raises an artifact hypothesis; inspect the evidence before accepting events.

series.title: Deflections aligned with the ECG reference
series.description: Invented values. One channel over 3 s; the large deflections land on the ECG R-peaks (shaded), about once per second.

simulations.title: Why Is the Cursor Drifting?
simulations.scenario: A synthetic cursor decoder was calibrated yesterday. Today, while the user rests, the cursor drifts upward. A two-minute check shows resting rates are about 15 % higher than yesterday on most channels, and the reach-minus-rest change on each channel matches yesterday's.
simulations.signalDescription: The plot shows today's decoded vertical velocity while the user rests: about +1.5 units/s instead of yesterday's 0. Modulation during reaches is unchanged.
simulations.decisionQuestion: What is the best next step?

choices.label: Schedule surgery to replace the electrodes
choices.rationale: Nothing here points to hardware failure: the channels still modulate as much as yesterday. An invasive step needs far stronger evidence.

choices.label: Increase the decoder gain
choices.rationale: Gain multiplies the offset along with the signal, so the resting drift would grow.

choices.label: Re-estimate resting baselines from a short rest block, subtract the shift, then re-check reaches
choices.rationale: A uniform rise at rest with unchanged modulation matches the additive-offset pattern. Correcting it is quick, needs no labels, and the re-check shows whether any other change remains.

choices.label: Stop using the BCI until the drift goes away
choices.rationale: This gives up control without testing the simplest explanation, which a two-minute correction could address.

simulations.oneLineMaster: When rest shifts but modulation does not, correct the offset first and re-check before anything more drastic.

simulations.title: The 90% Decoder That Doesn't Work
simulations.scenario: A fixed decoder matches 90% of offline direction labels, but live cursor target acquisition succeeds on 25% of attempts. You randomly split trials 80/20 after computing normalization parameters from the full dataset.
simulations.signalDescription: Offline direction-label accuracy = 90%; live target-acquisition success = 25%. These measure different outcomes and are not a single 65-percentage-point accuracy drop.
simulations.decisionQuestion: Which evaluation problem is directly established by the description?

choices.label: Full-data normalization used held-out information; rebuild and reassess the evaluation
choices.rationale: Fit normalization using the training subset only, then apply those parameters to held-out data. This corrects the stated leakage. It does not prove why live control performed poorly or establish overfitting.

choices.label: The patient is uncooperative
choices.rationale: Unsafe — blaming the user without ruling out methodology is wrong both ethically and scientifically.

choices.label: The cursor pixels are too small
choices.rationale: The description does not isolate display size as the cause. Offline label accuracy and live target acquisition are different endpoints.

choices.label: Surgery missed the target
choices.rationale: Unsafe and premature — you should fix evaluation methodology before revising surgery.

simulations.oneLineMaster: Separate training from evaluation before fitting preprocessing. Check that evaluation data and outcomes match the intended use; a random split alone does not establish leakage.

simulations.title: DBS Programming Trade-off
simulations.scenario: A Parkinson's patient's tremor responds well at 3.2 V on contact 1, but reports tingling in the contralateral hand and some slurred speech. Tremor is fully suppressed only at this amplitude.
simulations.signalDescription: Therapy window: tremor disappears at 2.6 V but returns within 20 seconds of rest. Side effects begin at 3.0 V.
simulations.decisionQuestion: Best programming change?

choices.label: Try a different contact or interleaved stimulation to widen the therapy window
choices.rationale: Correct — switching contacts shifts the current field and can decouple therapy from side effects.

choices.label: Increase amplitude further to overpower the side effects
choices.rationale: Unsafe — exceeds the side-effect threshold; charge density may approach safety limits.

choices.label: Turn the device off entirely
choices.rationale: Weaker — abandons known therapy without exploring tunable alternatives.

choices.label: Tell the patient to live with the slurring
choices.rationale: Unsafe and unethical — alternatives haven't been tried yet.

simulations.oneLineMaster: Widen the therapy window before pushing through side effects.

simulations.title: Trigger-Happy Detector
simulations.scenario: A synthetic responsive stimulator scores 1,000 decision windows a day. On review, 2 windows contained the target pattern and the device acted 80 times: both true events plus 78 false actions. The person reports frequent tingling from the extra stimulation. In this toy, the detector's settings are adjusted by the clinical team.
simulations.signalDescription: Sensitivity 2/2. False actions 78 of 998 non-event windows (about 7.8 %). Of 80 actions, 2 were correct: a positive predictive value of 2.5 %. In the plotted excerpt at threshold 5, four episodes start (circled) and only the one at index 7 overlaps the labeled event.
simulations.decisionQuestion: What is the best response?

choices.label: Lower the threshold to catch even more
choices.rationale: Both events are already detected; a lower threshold adds false actions and more unnecessary stimulation.

choices.label: Increase the stimulation amplitude
choices.rationale: This changes the action, not the decision. False actions would deliver more charge, not less.

choices.label: Turn detection off
choices.rationale: This removes the protection for real events. The problem is the operating point, not the existence of the detector.

choices.label: Raise the threshold, review the change with the clinical team, and track whether any true event is missed
choices.rationale: In the excerpt a threshold of 6 would keep the event at index 7 and drop the three brief crossings. On the full day that trade must be checked: fewer false actions may cost some sensitivity.

simulations.oneLineMaster: Convert error rates into actions per day before choosing a threshold, then watch the error you traded away.

simulations.title: Prosthetic Hand Without Sensation
simulations.scenario: A user with a myoelectric prosthesis can grip well in the lab. At home they crush eggs and drop heavier objects. They report exhaustion from constantly watching their hand.
simulations.signalDescription: Grip force is binary high/low with no proprioceptive feedback to the user.
simulations.decisionQuestion: Highest-impact improvement?

choices.label: Add graded sensory feedback (force and contact) via vibrotactile or peripheral nerve stim
choices.rationale: Correct — restoring feedback closes the loop and reduces visual attention load dramatically.

choices.label: Make the grip stronger by default
choices.rationale: Unsafe — stronger uncontrolled grip increases the crushing problem.

choices.label: Train the user to look more carefully
choices.rationale: Weaker — cognitive load is the bottleneck; more vigilance won't scale.

choices.label: Limit the prosthesis to flat objects
choices.rationale: Weaker — limits function without addressing the missing feedback channel.

simulations.oneLineMaster: When users have to watch a prosthesis, sensation is what's missing.

simulations.title: DBS Patient with New Symptoms
simulations.scenario: A long-time DBS patient calls reporting sudden return of tremor. They missed last week's medication refill and recently went through airport security.
simulations.signalDescription: Last clinic impedances normal. Device state: unknown remotely.
simulations.decisionQuestion: First step?

choices.label: Bring patient in to reproduce symptoms, verify device on/off state, check impedance, and review meds
choices.rationale: Correct — systematic differential before any parameter change.

choices.label: Immediately schedule revision surgery
choices.rationale: Unsafe — surgery without diagnosis.

choices.label: Tell the patient to double their amplitude at home
choices.rationale: Unsafe — uncontrolled change without diagnosis or supervision.

choices.label: Assume medication non-adherence and dismiss
choices.rationale: Weaker — could miss device-off-event from airport magnet or hardware issue.

simulations.oneLineMaster: Diagnose before you tune — implant troubleshooting is a differential, not a guess.

simulations.title: Reading a Firing Rate Model
simulations.scenario: A rate model of a decision-making circuit has two populations, each with τ = 100 ms, mutual inhibition, and self-excitation. After a step input the rates split: one rises, the other falls.
simulations.signalDescription: Within ~300 ms, one population stabilizes at high rate, the other near zero.
simulations.decisionQuestion: Which mechanism best explains the split?

choices.label: Winner-take-all attractor dynamics from mutual inhibition + self-excitation
choices.rationale: Correct — this is the canonical attractor mechanism for decisions.

choices.label: Hodgkin-Huxley action potentials at the population level
choices.rationale: Weaker — rate models abstract over spikes; HH is the wrong level of description.

choices.label: Synaptic depression alone
choices.rationale: Weaker — depression alone doesn't produce stable attractor states.

choices.label: Random noise without recurrent dynamics
choices.rationale: Weaker — noise alone wouldn't split into stable high/low states.

simulations.oneLineMaster: Mutual inhibition + self-excitation = winner-take-all — a decision attractor.

series.title: Two populations split after a step input
series.description: Invented rate-model output with time constant 100 ms. The step arrives at 0.05 s; within about 300 ms one population settles high and the other near zero.

simulations.title: Lesion in the Wrong Place?
simulations.scenario: A patient has profound naming difficulty after a small stroke. Their MRI shows a tiny lesion in the left thalamus — far from classic language cortex.
simulations.signalDescription: Lesion volume small; behavioral deficit large; canonical language cortex (Broca's, Wernicke's) is structurally intact.
simulations.decisionQuestion: Best interpretation?

choices.label: Diaschisis — the thalamic lesion disconnects or de-tunes intact language cortex through network effects
choices.rationale: Correct — distant lesions can produce large deficits via network connectivity.

choices.label: The MRI must be misread
choices.rationale: Weaker — assumes imaging error before considering network explanations.

choices.label: Language must be entirely in the thalamus
choices.rationale: Weaker — contradicts decades of lesion and stimulation evidence.

choices.label: The patient is malingering
choices.rationale: Unsafe — clinically inappropriate without thorough workup.

simulations.oneLineMaster: Distant lesions can cause big deficits — think networks, not just hotspots.

simulations.title: Signals Fade After 6 Months
simulations.scenario: A penetrating microelectrode array's signal-to-noise on most channels has dropped 40% over six months. Impedances have crept up. Patient reports no new symptoms.
simulations.signalDescription: Spike amplitude reduced; LFPs still measurable; impedance ~2× baseline on affected channels.
simulations.decisionQuestion: Most likely cause?

choices.label: Foreign-body response — glial encapsulation insulating the contacts
choices.rationale: Correct — slow rise in impedance with signal degradation is classic chronic encapsulation.

choices.label: Battery problem
choices.rationale: Weaker — recording quality issues with rising impedance aren't usually battery-related.

choices.label: Software bug in the decoder
choices.rationale: Weaker — software doesn't change impedance measurements.

choices.label: Electrode migration into ventricle
choices.rationale: Weaker — would show on imaging and typically presents more abruptly.

simulations.oneLineMaster: Slow impedance creep + amplitude drop = chronic tissue response, not a quick fix.

series.title: Spike amplitude after implantation
series.description: Invented weekly averages on one affected channel: amplitude falls over the first two months and then levels off, while field potentials stay measurable.

simulations.title: Choosing a Rehab Device
simulations.scenario: A stroke patient with partial hand function plateaus in outpatient therapy. They have motor cortex sparing but minimal voluntary finger extension. You can recommend one home device.
simulations.signalDescription: EMG shows some volitional activity; minimal finger extension; high motivation.
simulations.decisionQuestion: Best choice?

choices.label: BCI-FES or EMG-triggered FES for hand opening — pairs intent with movement
choices.rationale: Correct — closing the loop between intent and movement drives plasticity-relevant practice.

choices.label: Passive continuous motion device that moves the hand without patient effort
choices.rationale: Weaker — passive practice yields less plasticity than active engagement.

choices.label: No device — wait for spontaneous recovery
choices.rationale: Weaker — plasticity benefits from targeted practice during the recovery window.

choices.label: Major surgical intervention
choices.rationale: Unsafe — premature without trying lower-risk options.

simulations.oneLineMaster: Match the device to remaining intent — pairing volitional drive with movement is what builds recovery.

simulations.title: Selling Attention Scores
simulations.scenario: A synthetic wearable-EEG company offers free headsets to users who accept, in a sign-up click-through, that "aggregated attention scores" may be sold to advertisers and employers.
simulations.signalDescription: Continuous EEG; attention scores computed every minute; one click-through consent at sign-up, with no option to refuse the sale and keep the headset.
simulations.decisionQuestion: What is the strongest objection?

choices.label: The headset may be uncomfortable
choices.rationale: Comfort matters to users, but it is not the ethical core of selling inferences about their minds.

choices.label: Inferences about mental states go to third parties without specific, freely given and revocable consent
choices.rationale: Attention scores are inferences about a person's mind. A bundled click-through with no real choice is not specific consent, and selling them to employers creates risks the person cannot see or control.

choices.label: Advertisers will not pay much for the scores
choices.rationale: Whether the sale is profitable does not change whether it is acceptable.

choices.label: EEG cannot measure attention at all
choices.rationale: This overstates the science. The objection does not depend on how accurate the scores are; inaccurate scores sold to employers would add further harm.

simulations.oneLineMaster: Inferences about mental states need specific, freely given, revocable consent before anyone else sees them.

simulations.title: Cursor: Why Is the Start So Steady?
simulations.scenario: A toy cursor starts at 0 with a target at 1. Each 0.1 s update sets velocity = 8 × (target - position), clips it to a 2 units/s speed limit, and moves by velocity × 0.1. There is no delay and no noise.

choices.label: The decoder is noisy at the start
choices.rationale: The model is deterministic. Equal steps come from a rule, not from noise.

choices.label: The gain of 8 is too low to move faster
choices.rationale: An unclipped command of 8 units/s would cover 0.8 units in the first step. The limit, not the gain, sets the early speed.

neuroCodeLessons.title: Features: Mean, RMS and a Sample Count
neuroCodeLessons.explanation: Mean and root mean square (RMS) summarize different properties. For N samples, RMS is the square root of the mean of their squares. Both have the input units. The number of samples strictly above the mean is a dimensionless count and is not signal energy.
neuroCodeLessons.challengePrompt: Define window_features(samples). Return [mean, rms, count_above_mean]. The count uses strictly greater than, not greater than or equal to. Raise ValueError for an empty list. Retain the original input list. Inputs are finite numerical values.
neuroCodeLessons.hint: Compute the mean once, square values before averaging for RMS, then count values greater than that mean.
neuroCodeLessons.solution:
def window_features(samples):
    if not samples:
        raise ValueError("At least one sample is required")
    mean = sum(samples) / len(samples)
    rms = (sum(value * value for value in samples) / len(samples)) ** 0.5
    count = sum(value > mean for value in samples)
    return [mean, rms, count]

print(window_features([2, -1, 8, 3, -2, 9, 1, 4]))
neuroCodeLessons.oneLineMaster: Mean and root mean square (RMS) summarize different properties.

neuroCodeLessons.explanation: Each inner list holds one channel's spike counts in consecutive bins of equal length. neuroCodeLessons.title: Confirmation: Act Only After N Windows in a Row
neuroCodeLessons.explanation: A confirmation rule acts only when a detector value stays at or above threshold for n consecutive windows. It fires once per run, at the window where the run reaches length n, and re-arms only after a value falls below threshold. Brief deflections are filtered out; the price is a known delay of n - 1 windows. This toy rule does not establish that any real stimulation policy is safe.

Each run fires at most once; a value below threshold resets the run. Raise ValueError unless n is an integer of at least 1. With n = 1 the result is the first index of each run. Do not change the input list.
neuroCodeLessons.hint: Keep a counter: add 1 for each qualifying value, reset to 0 otherwise, and record the index when the counter equals n.

neuroCodeLessons.title: Graded Speed: Slow Down When Unsure
neuroCodeLessons.neuroengineeringConcept: Showing decoder uncertainty in the interface
neuroCodeLessons.explanation: Instead of jumping between full speed and a stop, the cursor speed can grow with the score's distance from the threshold, reaching full speed at the margin. The user sees the cursor slow as the evidence weakens. Direction follows the sign of score minus threshold; exactly at the threshold the speed is zero.
neuroCodeLessons.challengePrompt: Define graded_speed(score, threshold, margin, full_speed). Let d = score - threshold. Return full_speed × min(1, |d| / margin), positive when d > 0 and negative when d < 0 (zero when d is zero). Raise ValueError when margin is zero or negative, or full_speed is negative.
neuroCodeLessons.hint: Compute the unsigned speed first, then return its negative when d < 0.
neuroCodeLessons.solution:
def graded_speed(score, threshold, margin, full_speed):
    if margin <= 0 or full_speed < 0:
        raise ValueError("margin must be positive and full_speed non-negative")
    d = score - threshold
    speed = full_speed * min(1, abs(d) / margin)
    return -speed if d < 0 else speed

print(graded_speed(0.1, 0, 0.5, 4))
neuroCodeLessons.oneLineMaster: Let the cursor's speed show how sure the decoder is.

neuroCodeLessons.title: Capstone: Baseline to Cursor in One Function
neuroCodeLessons.codingConcept: Composing functions and returning intermediate results
neuroCodeLessons.explanation: Four stages from earlier units, chained: subtract each channel's baseline, count threshold episodes per channel, compute a weighted score with an explicit tie rule, then move the cursor one step right or left. Returning the features and labels as well as the positions makes every stage inspectable. This is a toy batch pipeline on invented numbers, not a live decoder.
neuroCodeLessons.codeExample:
def count_episodes(samples, threshold):
    count, previous_above = 0, False
    for sample in samples:
        above = sample >= threshold
        if above and not previous_above:
            count += 1
        previous_above = above
    return count

def toy_pipeline(trials, baselines, threshold, weights, bias, step):
    return {"features": [], "labels": [], "positions": [0]}  # Chain the four stages

trials = [[[10, 17, 11, 16, 10], [20, 21, 20, 22, 20]],
          [[10, 11, 10, 10, 12], [20, 27, 26, 20, 28]],
          [[10, 16, 10, 10, 10], [20, 26, 20, 20, 20]]]
print(toy_pipeline(trials, [10, 20], 5, [-1, 1], 0, 1))
neuroCodeLessons.challengePrompt: Define toy_pipeline(trials, baselines, threshold, weights, bias, step). Each trial holds exactly two channels of samples. For each trial: subtract baselines[c] from every sample of channel c; count episodes at or above threshold on each corrected channel with count_episodes; score = weights[0] × count0 + weights[1] × count1 + bias; label "right" only when the score is above 0, otherwise "left". Positions start at [0]; each trial appends the previous position plus step for right or minus step for left. Return a dictionary with keys features (one [count0, count1] per trial), labels and positions. Raise ValueError when baselines or weights do not have exactly two values, step is not positive, or a trial does not have exactly two channels. Do not change the inputs.
neuroCodeLessons.hint: Build the corrected channel as a new list: [s - baselines[c] for s in channel]. Append to positions with positions[-1] + step or positions[-1] - step.

1.whyItMatters: Neurons receive and transmit signals through electrical and chemical processes. A membrane voltage is measured across the cell membrane; an extracellular electrode measures voltage outside cells. Before calculating features, identify what was measured and how each sample maps to time.
1.shortLesson: A time series needs ordered measurements, units and timing. For equally spaced samples, time at index i is start time + i / sampling rate. A list alone does not tell us the sampling rate. Intracellular membrane voltage and extracellular electrode voltage are different measurements; do not transfer their thresholds or amplitudes between recordings. Extracellular signals can be processed to study rapid events or slower field activity. Detecting an event does not by itself identify a neuron.
1.mentalModel: Think of neural data like a movie made of voltage frames. One frame is rarely enough; the pattern across frames is what the decoder reads.
1.workedExample: Synthetic membrane-voltage example: [-70, -68, -45, -42, -70] mV, sampled at 1,000 samples/second starting at 0 seconds. Index 2 occurs at 2/1,000 = 0.002 seconds. The first-to-last timestamp span is 4 milliseconds. This short toy list is not a validated spike recording.

2.whyItMatters: Spike detection is often the first transformation from raw voltage to useful neural events. Bad thresholds create fake spikes or miss real ones.
2.shortLesson: A positive-threshold event starts when a sample reaches or exceeds a chosen level after the previous sample was below it. Consecutive above-threshold samples belong to one continuous episode in this toy detector. We assume the trace starts below threshold; an above-threshold first sample is counted as one episode by convention. Real detection also needs recording context, waveform checks and handling of artifacts and repeated detections. An event is not automatically a physiological spike or an identified neuron.
2.mentalModel: Count entries through a gate, not every moment spent beyond the gate. A more permissive threshold can admit more unwanted events. Which numerical direction is permissive depends on detection polarity.
2.workedExample: Synthetic membrane-voltage samples [-70, -55, -42, -66, -44, -39, -71] mV contain three samples at or above -50 mV, but only two above-threshold episodes. At -40 mV only the -39 sample qualifies, so the episode count is one. These are toy threshold events, not confirmed spikes.

4.whyItMatters: BCI code can only decode intent if the input signal is actually related to intent. Noise and artifacts can make a decoder learn the wrong relationship.
4.shortLesson: A useful signal depends on the question being asked. Movement, muscle activity, electrical interference and electrode instability can contaminate a recording. An artifact correlated with task labels may look predictive during training. Compare raw traces, reference channels, timing and recording conditions before interpreting a detected event. A numerical threshold is only one observation.
4.mentalModel: Noise is like static over a radio message. The message may still be there, but the code needs to know what not to trust.

5.whyItMatters: Filtering and smoothing prepare the signal so feature extraction sees the relevant pattern instead of avoidable noise.
5.shortLesson: A filter transforms a signal. A centered three-sample moving average replaces a middle value with the average of itself and its two neighbors. It changes genuine events as well as unwanted variation. Here we output only centers with the center and both neighbors available. A list of N samples produces N-2 values when N is at least 3; shorter lists produce no full-window averages. Boundary handling and timing conventions belong in the method description.
5.mentalModel: Filtering is a lens. It can make the target clearer, but the wrong lens can blur away the thing you need.
5.workedExample: For synthetic values [10, 12, 50, 13, 11], the full-window centered averages are [24, 25, 24.6667]. The middle output is (12 + 50 + 13) / 3 = 25. A real narrow peak would also be reduced; a smoother plot is not evidence that only noise was removed.

activeRecallPrompts.hint: Think timing and sharp peaks.

6.whyItMatters: A decoder never sees the raw trace. It sees the few numbers you chose to compute from each window, so anything those numbers discard is invisible to every later stage.
6.shortLesson: A feature is a number computed from a window of samples; a feature vector is the short list of such numbers passed to a decoder. Each feature keeps one property of the window and throws the rest away. The mean keeps the signed average level, so a constant offset changes it. Root mean square (RMS) is the square root of the mean of the squared samples. It keeps overall size and discards sign, so it is never negative. A threshold count, such as the number of samples at or above a level, keeps whether large values occurred but not their exact size or timing. All three carry the input units except the count, which is dimensionless. Two windows can share a mean and an RMS yet differ in ways a decoder needs, such as one brief large deflection versus a steady oscillation. Choosing features is therefore a choice about which differences you believe matter for the task. A feature that separates training windows is a candidate, not evidence of a neural cause: an offset from electrode drift or an artifact correlated with the task can separate windows just as well.
6.mentalModel: Each feature is a question you ask the window. Mean asks "where is the average level?", RMS asks "how big is it overall?", a count asks "how often did it get large?". The decoder can only use the answers, never the window.
6.workedExample: Two synthetic 10-sample windows in microvolts. Window A: [1, 0, -1, 10, -5, -5, 2, 0, -2, 0]. Window B: [4, -4, 4, -4, 4, -4, 4, -4, 4, -4]. Both sums are 0, so both means are 0 µV. Squares in A add to 1 + 1 + 100 + 25 + 25 + 4 + 4 = 160; every square in B is 16, also 160 in total. Both RMS values are the square root of 160 / 10 = 16, which is 4 µV. Counting samples at or above +8 µV gives 1 for A (the 10) and 0 for B. Mean and RMS cannot tell these windows apart; the count can. Whether that count reflects neural activity is a separate question this calculation does not answer.

activeRecallPrompts.prompt: Why can RMS never be negative, even for a window of all-negative samples?
activeRecallPrompts.hint: Look at the operations inside the definition.
activeRecallPrompts.answer: Every sample is squared before averaging, and the square root of a non-negative mean is non-negative. The sign of the samples is discarded.

activeRecallPrompts.prompt: Windows A and B have equal mean and equal RMS. What does a decoder that sees only those two features know about the difference between them?
activeRecallPrompts.hint: A decoder only receives the feature values.
activeRecallPrompts.answer: Nothing. Identical feature vectors look identical to the decoder, so any difference between the windows has to be captured by another feature.

6.commonMistake: Adding many overlapping features and assuming the model will sort out which ones matter, without checking what each one keeps and discards.
6.masteryCriteria: You can compute mean, RMS and a threshold count for a short window by hand, say what each one discards, and construct two windows that one feature separates and another does not.

7.whyItMatters: A decoder is the step where numbers become a command. Writing that step as an explicit rule lets you trace every output back to the features, weights and tie rule that produced it.
7.shortLesson: The simplest decoder computes a score from the feature vector and compares it with zero. A linear score multiplies each feature by a weight, adds the products and adds a bias: score = w0·f0 + w1·f1 + b. A positive score maps to one label and everything else to the other. The set of feature vectors where the score is exactly zero is the decision boundary; for two features it is a straight line. Weights set the boundary's orientation and the bias shifts it. Three details decide whether the rule is fully specified. First, the tie rule: what happens at exactly zero. Without one, two programs can disagree on the same input. Second, the sign convention: "right" for positive scores is an engineering choice, not a property of the brain. Flipping every weight and the bias swaps the labels. Third, units: each weight is in label-score units per feature unit, so changing a feature from hertz to spikes per window changes the weight needed. A rule that labels training rows well has learned a boundary for those rows. Whether it holds on new trials is a separate test (Unit 10 in this module).
7.mentalModel: Draw the two features as axes. The decoder is a straight fence across that plane. Points on one side get one label; points on the fence itself go wherever the tie rule sends them.
7.workedExample: Features are a left-channel rate f0 and a right-channel rate f1, in Hz. Weights [-1, 1] and bias 0 give score = f1 - f0, labeled right when the score is above 0. Trial [12, 20]: score 8, right. Trial [18, 9]: score -9, left. Trial [15, 15]: score 0, left by the tie rule. Now set the bias to -5, so right needs f1 - f0 above 5. Trial [12, 20] scores 8 - 5 = 3 and stays right. Trial [14, 17] scores 3 - 5 = -2 and becomes left. The bias moved the fence 5 Hz toward the right-channel side. All rates are invented.

figure.title: Moving the fence with the bias
figure.description: With bias 0 the fence is f1 = f0. Setting the bias to -5 moves it to f1 = f0 + 5. Trial [14, 17] sits between the two fences: right with bias 0, left with bias -5.

activeRecallPrompts.prompt: Why does a decoder need an explicit tie rule?
activeRecallPrompts.hint: Think about a score of exactly zero.
activeRecallPrompts.answer: Without one, the label for a zero score depends on how the comparison happens to be written, so two implementations can disagree on the same input.

activeRecallPrompts.prompt: What happens to every label if you multiply both weights and the bias by -1?
activeRecallPrompts.hint: Each score changes sign.
activeRecallPrompts.answer: Every nonzero score flips sign, so right and left swap. Scores of exactly zero stay zero and keep the tie-rule label.

7.commonMistake: Reading the decoder's "right" label as the person's intention, when it is a rule-defined label on synthetic or recorded features.
7.masteryCriteria: You can compute a linear score and label by hand, apply the tie rule, explain what weights and bias do to the decision boundary, and predict the effect of flipping signs.

8.whyItMatters: In a cursor BCI the decoder output is not the end of the pipeline. It moves something the user watches, and what the user sees shapes the next neural activity the decoder receives.
8.shortLesson: Many intracortical cursor BCIs decode a velocity rather than a position; the high-performance decoder of Gilja and colleagues (2012) is one example. At each update the decoded velocity is multiplied by the update interval dt and added to the current position: x[t+1] = x[t] + v[t]·dt. Most systems clip the velocity to a maximum speed so that one noisy window cannot throw the cursor across the screen. The loop then closes through the person. They see where the cursor is, compare it with where they want it, and their next attempt changes the neural activity the decoder sees. This makes the system a feedback loop with a human in it. Three consequences follow. Errors in velocity accumulate into position, so a small constant bias becomes steady drift. The speed limit trades responsiveness for safety and smoothness. And the user adapts to the decoder while the engineer adapts the decoder to the user, so performance measured with one decoder version does not transfer automatically to another.
8.mentalModel: The decoder is a steering wheel, not a teleport. It sets how fast the cursor moves for the next fraction of a second; the person watches and steers again.
8.workedExample: Update interval dt = 0.05 s, speed limit 4 units/s, start at x = 0. Decoded velocities for three updates: 2, 6 and -1 units/s. Step 1: 0 + 2 × 0.05 = 0.10. Step 2: 6 is clipped to 4, so 0.10 + 4 × 0.05 = 0.30. Step 3: 0.30 - 1 × 0.05 = 0.25. A constant decoding bias of 0.2 units/s while the user rests would add 0.2 × 0.05 = 0.01 units every step, or 0.2 units every second. Reaching a target 1 unit away at the full 4 units/s takes 1 / 4 = 0.25 s, five updates of 0.05 s; with a 2 units/s limit it takes ten updates. Numbers are synthetic and the model has no delay; Unit 12 adds one.

9.whyItMatters: The recorded signals change within a day and across days. A decoder calibrated yesterday can push the cursor somewhere the user did not intend today, and the cheapest fix depends on what kind of change happened.
9.shortLesson: Calibration fits a decoder's parameters, such as each channel's baseline and the weights, using data recorded while the intended action is known. Drift is any later change in the relationship between features and intent. Perge and colleagues (2013) found that signal changes within a single day measurably reduced decoding performance in people with intracortical arrays. Causes include small electrode movements, tissue responses, changes in attention or fatigue, and changes in which neurons are near each electrode. Three simple drift signatures need different responses. An additive offset shifts a feature by a constant: rest and movement values both rise by the same amount. A gain change scales how much the feature moves with intent. A tuning change alters which direction or action a channel responds to. Subtracting the change in resting baseline corrects only the first. It needs a short rest block, no labels and little time, which is why it is often the first step. If the cursor stops drifting at rest but movements are still too small or point the wrong way, the remaining error is not an offset, and a calibration block with known targets is needed.
9.mentalModel: Think of a bathroom scale. An offset is a scale that reads 2 kg heavy for everyone: subtract 2. A gain error reads 10 % heavy: subtraction cannot fix it. Check which kind of error you have before choosing the fix.
9.workedExample: One synthetic channel, yesterday: rest 12 Hz, reaching 32 Hz, so the modulation is 20 Hz. Today: rest 17 Hz. With an unchanged decoder weight of 0.1 (units/s per Hz), the 5 Hz offset produces 0.1 × 5 = 0.5 units/s of drift while the user rests. Subtracting the shift: corrected = observed - (17 - 12). A reach today reads 27 Hz, corrected to 22 Hz, so the corrected modulation is 22 - 12 = 10 Hz. Resting drift is gone, but the reach modulation is half of yesterday's 20 Hz. The additive model fixed the offset and exposed a gain change it cannot correct.

figure.description: Today's rest is 5 Hz higher. Subtracting 5 Hz removes the resting drift, but the corrected reach is only 10 Hz above rest, half of yesterday's 20 Hz modulation.

activeRecallPrompts.prompt: Why is re-estimating the resting baseline a sensible first step when drift appears?
activeRecallPrompts.hint: Compare its cost and risk with a full calibration.
activeRecallPrompts.answer: It needs only a short rest block, no labels and no change to the weights. If an offset explains the drift it restores control quickly; if not, the remaining error points to what to fix next.

9.commonMistake: Calling every performance drop a hardware failure, or every drift an offset, without checking rest and movement values separately.
9.masteryCriteria: You can apply an additive baseline correction by hand, tell offset, gain and tuning changes apart from rest and movement values, and choose a first recalibration step with its limits stated.

10.whyItMatters: When a system acts on its own detections, error rates become events per day that someone experiences. A rule that looks accurate on paper can still act wrongly dozens of times a day.
10.shortLesson: A closed-loop neurotechnology system senses a signal, decides whether a condition is present, acts, and then senses again, so its own action can change what it measures next. Responsive neurostimulation for epilepsy is a clinical example: the implant detects programmed electrographic patterns and delivers brief stimulation (Morrell, 2011). Two error types matter. A false positive acts when the condition is absent; a false negative misses it. Sensitivity is the fraction of true events detected. Specificity is the fraction of non-events correctly ignored. The trap is base rate. A detector usually checks many short windows, and almost all of them are non-events. Even 99 % specificity then produces many false actions, and most actions may be false even though each one looked unlikely. The positive predictive value, the fraction of actions that were correct, falls as events become rarer. Designers therefore also gate actions with conditions that do not depend on the detector, such as a device being armed or a power supply being adequate, and they decide which error is worse before choosing a threshold.
10.mentalModel: A smoke alarm in a kitchen. It checks the air every second of every day; even a rare false alarm per check adds up to many false alarms per week. How often it checks and how rare real fires are matter as much as how good each single check is.
10.workedExample: A synthetic detector checks 10-second windows: 8,640 per day. 20 windows contain the target pattern; 8,620 do not. Sensitivity 90 % detects 0.9 × 20 = 18 events. Specificity 99 % still flags 1 % of 8,620, about 86 windows. Of roughly 104 actions, 18 are correct: a positive predictive value near 17 %. Raising specificity to 99.9 % cuts false actions to about 9, if sensitivity can be kept. A gating condition, such as acting only while the device is armed, leaves these detection counts unchanged; it limits when a detection may become an action. These counts are invented for practice.

11.whyItMatters: The person using a BCI learns from what the interface shows them. An interface that hides uncertainty or changes behavior silently makes the whole system harder to control, however good the decoder is.
11.shortLesson: The interface is part of the control loop. What it shows, and when, changes what the user tries next. Several design choices follow. Show uncertainty in a form the user can act on: slowing the cursor as the score approaches the threshold tells the user, without words, that the system is unsure, and invites a stronger or clearer attempt. Graded speed of this kind is a continuous cousin of the abstain rule in Unit 15. Make changes visible: when the system recalibrates or adapts, say so, say what changed, and allow it to be undone. Protect control: a stop or pause that works through a separate input should always be available, so a misbehaving decoder cannot trap the user. Respect fatigue: performance and comfort change across a session, and long calibrations cost the user's time and energy. Measure what matters to the user, such as correct selections per minute including the time spent undoing errors, not only decoder accuracy. Clinical BCI studies report outcomes like typing rates for this reason (Pandarinath et al., 2017). None of these choices make the decoder more accurate; they make the person and the system easier to coordinate.
11.mentalModel: The screen is a conversation, not a scoreboard. Every movement says something to the user about how sure the system is.
11.workedExample: Graded speed with threshold 0, margin 0.5 and full speed 4 units/s: speed = 4 × min(1, |score| / 0.5), in the direction of the score's sign. Score 0.1 gives 4 × 0.2 = 0.8 units/s. Score -0.3 gives -(4 × 0.6) = -2.4 units/s. Score 0.9 is beyond the margin and gives the full 4 units/s. At 0.8 units/s, crossing 1 unit takes 1 / 0.8 = 1.25 s, slow enough to notice. Throughput: 10 selections in 60 s with 2 wrong, each needing a 5 s undo, gives 8 correct in 60 s = 8 per minute; it is not 10.

12.whyItMatters: Neural data can support inferences about attention, mood or health that the person never meant to share. What a system collects, keeps and passes on is a design decision made long before anyone misuses it.
12.shortLesson: Brain data raise the ordinary privacy questions with higher stakes. Recordings and the features computed from them can support inferences beyond their original purpose, and the person may not be able to tell what is being inferred. Ethicists have argued for explicit protections of mental privacy and agency (Yuste et al., 2017) and for rights specific to neurotechnology (Ienca and Andorno, 2017). Several practical principles follow, and some also appear in data-protection law such as the EU's GDPR. Purpose limitation: state what the data are for and use them only for that. Data minimization: collect and keep only what that purpose needs. Specific, revocable consent: the person agrees to particular uses, can understand them and can withdraw. Retention limits: delete what is no longer needed. Access control: limit and log who can see the data. Minimization is often a technical choice. Sending computed features instead of raw recordings cuts the data volume dramatically. Smaller is not automatically safe, though: features can still reveal states the person did not mean to share, so the purpose test applies to them too. A code filter that drops fields is one protective measure; it does not establish consent, anonymity or legal compliance by itself.
12.mentalModel: Treat a neural recording like a diary that writes itself. Ask what each page is for before you keep it, and who else could read something you did not mean to say.

Features instead: 2 numbers per channel per 20 ms bin is 96 × 2 = 192 numbers per bin; 50 bins per second makes 9,600 numbers per second, × 4 bytes = 38,400 bytes per second. That is 150 times less data (5,760,000 / 38,400 = 150). The features still describe moment-to-moment activity on every channel, so they still need a stated purpose and consent.

13.whyItMatters: Single channels are noisy and can stop working. Decoders combine many channels into one vector so that intent is read from the pattern across the population rather than from any one recording site.
13.shortLesson: A population vector, in the classic sense, comes from recordings in which each neuron fires most for one movement direction, its preferred direction. Each neuron votes for its preferred direction, weighted by how far its rate is above or below its own baseline; the sum of the votes points in the decoded direction. Georgopoulos and colleagues showed in 1986 that this sum tracked arm-movement direction in monkey motor cortex. Today the term is often used loosely for the feature vector: one number per channel or unit (a rate, a threshold-crossing count) at one time step. Most modern decoders apply learned weights to that vector rather than assuming a direction per neuron, but the idea is the same: a fixed linear combination across many channels. Combining channels helps because independent noise partly cancels. If each of N channels has independent noise with standard deviation s, their average has standard deviation s divided by the square root of N. Noise that is shared across channels, such as a common reference artifact, does not cancel this way. A population readout also degrades gradually: losing one channel shortens or bends the vector instead of erasing it.
13.mentalModel: Each channel is one noisy voter with a fixed direction. The vote is the sum of everyone's arrows. A few voters going quiet makes the result weaker, not random.
13.workedExample: Four synthetic channels prefer right, up, left and down. Each has a baseline of 10 Hz. One 100 ms window gives rates [30, 20, 10, 0] Hz, so the modulations are [+20, +10, 0, -10] Hz. Horizontal component: right minus left = 20 - 0 = 20. Vertical component: up minus down = 10 - (-10) = 20. The vector (20, 20) points up and to the right at 45 degrees. Noise: if each channel's rate had independent noise with standard deviation 4 Hz, the average of the four channels would have 4 / 2 = 2 Hz, because the square root of 4 is 2. These numbers are invented; real tuning is broader and noise is partly shared.

figure.title: Four tuned channels in one window
figure.description: Rates minus the 10 Hz baseline give modulations of +20, +10, 0 and -10 Hz. Right minus left is 20, up minus down is 20, so the population vector points up and to the right.

activeRecallPrompts.prompt: Why does averaging four channels halve the noise standard deviation only when the noise is independent?
activeRecallPrompts.hint: Think about what happens when every channel jumps up together.
activeRecallPrompts.answer: Independent fluctuations partly cancel in the average. Shared fluctuations move every channel together, so the average moves with them and does not shrink by the square root of N.

activeRecallPrompts.prompt: If the "up" channel in the worked example stops modulating, what happens to the population vector?
activeRecallPrompts.hint: Recompute with that channel at baseline.
activeRecallPrompts.answer: Its +10 Hz vote becomes 0, so the vertical component falls from 20 to 10. The vector still points up and right but is shorter and tilted toward right: the readout degrades rather than fails.

13.commonMistake: Treating one strongly tuned channel as the signal and the rest as clutter, then losing control when that channel drifts or fails.
13.masteryCriteria: You can compute a population vector from rates, baselines and preferred directions, state the square-root-of-N noise rule and its independence assumption, and predict what a lost channel does to the readout.

14.whyItMatters: A weighted linear decoder is still widely used because it is fast, needs little data and can be inspected. Inspection only helps if you know what a weight does and does not tell you, and if your accuracy number was measured honestly.
14.shortLesson: A weighted linear decoder computes score = w·f + b over many features and applies a fixed rule to the score. Weights are usually fitted on training data, for example by least squares or ridge regression; ridge adds a penalty that keeps weights small when data are limited or features are correlated. Two habits make the result trustworthy. First, read contributions, not raw weights. A feature's contribution to the score is its weight times its value. A tiny weight on a feature measured in large units can matter more than a large weight on a feature measured in small units. Standardizing features to comparable scales before fitting makes weight sizes easier to compare. Second, keep three kinds of data apart. Training data choose the weights. Validation data choose between candidate settings, such as the ridge penalty or which features to keep. Test data are used once, after every choice is fixed, to estimate performance on new trials. Any choice made by looking at test results turns the test set into part of training, and the reported accuracy becomes optimistic. Accuracy on a few rows is also uncertain: 4/4 correct says little about the next hundred trials.
14.mentalModel: Weights are exchange rates between each feature's units and the score. To see who is driving the decision, convert every feature into score units first, then compare.
14.workedExample: Features: firing rate f0 in Hz and RMS f1 in µV. Weights [0.05, 4.0], bias -3. Trial [40 Hz, 0.3 µV]: contributions are 0.05 × 40 = 2.0 and 4.0 × 0.3 = 1.2, so the score is 2.0 + 1.2 - 3 = 0.2, labeled right. The rate drives the decision more, although its weight is 80 times smaller. If you choose among 20 candidate weight vectors by their accuracy on 4 test rows and report the best, that number is no longer a test result; a fresh, untouched set is needed. All values are synthetic.

figure.description: Each feature contributes weight × value. The rate term (2.0) outweighs the RMS term (1.2), even though its weight is 80 times smaller. With the bias of -3 the score is 0.2: right.

activeRecallPrompts.hint: Multiply before comparing.
activeRecallPrompts.answer: Contribution is weight times value. A feature measured in large units can produce a large contribution with a small weight.

activeRecallPrompts.prompt: You picked the decoder with the best test accuracy out of 20 tries. What should you report, and what do you still need?
activeRecallPrompts.hint: The test set made a choice.
activeRecallPrompts.answer: Report it as a validation result. An honest test estimate needs a separate set that played no part in any choice.

14.commonMistake: Ranking features by raw weight size, or tuning on the test set and reporting the best number as test accuracy.
14.masteryCriteria: You can compute contributions and a score by hand, explain why standardization helps weight inspection, and describe a training, validation and test split that keeps the final estimate honest.

15.whyItMatters: Recalibrating from scratch every day costs the user time and attention. Adaptive systems try to keep the decoder aligned with the smallest, safest update that fixes the observed change.
15.shortLesson: Online adaptation updates decoder parameters during or between sessions. A useful ladder runs from cheap to expensive. First, per-channel offsets: re-estimate each channel's resting mean from a short rest block, with no labels. Second, per-channel scales: re-estimate how much each channel moves with intent, which needs a short block with known targets. Third, the weights themselves: a full recalibration. Normalizing each feature as (value - resting mean) / scale lets the weights stay fixed while offsets and scales are updated. A slow tracker can follow gradual change without stopping the user. An exponential moving average updates a running estimate m toward each new value x by a fraction a: m_new = m + a × (x - m). Small a changes slowly and resists noise; large a follows quickly but also follows anything else. That is the risk of unsupervised tracking: if the user holds one intention for a long time, the tracker can absorb it into the "baseline" and weaken the very command the user is producing. Published approaches range from self-recalibration during use (Jarosiewicz et al., 2015) and closed-loop decoder adaptation (Orsborn et al., 2014) to aligning low-dimensional neural activity across days (Degenhart et al., 2020).
15.mentalModel: Tune the instrument before you rewrite the music. Fix offsets, then scales, and rewrite the weights only when the tune itself has changed.
15.workedExample: One synthetic channel yesterday: resting mean 20 Hz, scale 20 Hz, so a 40 Hz reach normalizes to (40 - 20) / 20 = 1.0. Today rest is 26 Hz and a reach reads 36 Hz. Updating only the mean gives (36 - 26) / 20 = 0.5. Updating the scale to today's 10 Hz modulation gives (36 - 26) / 10 = 1.0 again, with the weights untouched. Tracking: a running mean m = 20 with a = 0.1 and a new rest value 26 becomes 20 + 0.1 × 6 = 20.6; another 26 gives 20.6 + 0.1 × 5.4 = 21.14.

figure.title: A running mean catching up
figure.description: Each update moves the mean a tenth of the way toward today's rest of 26 Hz: 20, 20.6, 21.14 and so on. Tracking is gradual by design, so one noisy window cannot yank the baseline.

activeRecallPrompts.answer: It slowly absorbs the sustained activity into the baseline, so the normalized feature shrinks and the command the user is producing weakens.

15.commonMistake: Refitting every weight whenever performance drops, or letting an unsupervised tracker run with no check on what it is absorbing.
15.masteryCriteria: You can normalize a feature with an offset and scale, update a running estimate with an exponential moving average by hand, and choose the cheapest recalibration step that matches an observed change.

16.whyItMatters: Every stage between a neural event and the cursor adds delay. In a feedback loop, delay does more than slow things down: corrections based on old information keep pushing after they should stop, and the cursor overshoots.
16.shortLesson: End-to-end latency is the time from a change in neural activity to a visible change in the output. It is a budget made of stages: the length of the window used to compute features, filtering, decoding, transmission, and the display refresh. Some stages are fixed costs; others are design choices. Shorter feature windows reduce delay but contain fewer spikes, so rate estimates get noisier. In a closed loop, delay changes behavior. The person corrects toward the target based on where the cursor appears to be. If that view is old, the correction continues after the cursor has already arrived, and the cursor overshoots and swings back. A lower controller gain reduces overshoot but makes movement sluggish. Cunningham and colleagues (2011) built a closed-loop simulator to study exactly these interactions between decoder, delay and human feedback. People also adapt. In monkeys using a BCI, Golub and colleagues (2015) found neural activity consistent with an internal model that partly compensates for feedback delay, and the feedback control of people using intracortical BCIs has been modeled directly (Willett and colleagues, 2017). Compensation is partial, so engineers still treat latency as a budget to defend.
16.mentalModel: Steering by a video feed that is a fifth of a second behind. You keep turning after you are already lined up, then have to turn back.
16.workedExample: A synthetic budget: 50 ms feature window, 5 ms filter, 2 ms decode, 10 ms radio link, up to 17 ms waiting for a 60 Hz display refresh. Total: 50 + 5 + 2 + 10 + 17 = 84 ms. With a 100 ms budget, 16 ms remain. A cursor moving at 2 units/s travels 2 × 0.084 = 0.168 units during that delay. Now a toy loop: the cursor moves toward a target at 1.0 with velocity 5 × (target - observed position), updated every 0.1 s. Without delay the positions are 0, 0.5, 0.75, 0.875: the error halves each step. If the observed position is 0.2 s old, the positions are 0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 1.75, 1.75, 1.5: the cursor passes the target and comes back.

figure.description: Velocity is 5 × (target − observed position), updated every 0.1 s. Without delay the error halves each step. When the observed position is 0.2 s old, the cursor passes the target and swings back.

16.masteryCriteria: You can add up a latency budget, state what each stage trades away, and explain with numbers why delayed feedback makes a cursor overshoot.

17.whyItMatters: A decoder that must answer every window will act on its weakest evidence. Letting it say "not sure" can prevent many wrong actions, at the price of acting less often.
17.shortLesson: A linear score carries more than its sign: a score near the threshold rests on weak evidence, while one far away rests on strong evidence, at least for the data the decoder was fitted on. An abstain rule turns that into a third output. Within a margin around the threshold the decoder abstains; outside it, it labels as usual. Two numbers then describe performance. Coverage is the fraction of windows on which the system acts. Selective accuracy is the accuracy among those acted windows. Widening the margin usually raises selective accuracy and lowers coverage. Distance from the threshold is not a calibrated probability: a score can be far from the threshold and still be wrong, for example when drift moved the features. Calibration methods map scores to probabilities that can be checked against outcomes. Graceful degradation is the plan for when abstaining persists. A system that has abstained for several seconds should hold still, say plainly that it is unsure, and offer a recalibration or another input rather than quietly lowering its standards. Abstaining is a decision layer; how the interface shows uncertainty is the subject of Unit 17.
17.mentalModel: A careful driver at a confusing junction slows down and checks before turning. Stopping is a real option, not a failure, but stopping forever is not driving either. The margin sets how confusing a junction has to be before the driver stops.
17.workedExample: Ten synthetic windows, threshold 0, right above 0. Scores [2.1, 1.4, 0.3, -0.2, -1.8, -2.5, 0.4, -0.4, 1.9, -1.1]; true labels [R, R, L, R, L, L, R, L, L, L]. Acting on all ten gives 7 correct; counting from 1, windows 3, 4 and 9 are wrong. With a margin of 0.5, windows 3, 4, 7 and 8 abstain, because their scores are within 0.5 of 0. The six acted windows give 5 correct: selective accuracy 5/6 ≈ 83 % at 60 % coverage. Two errors were avoided, two correct actions were lost, and window 9 is still a confident error.

activeRecallPrompts.answer: Distance only reflects the fitted rule. Drift, artifacts or a poor fit can produce confident wrong scores; only checking against outcomes shows whether confidence is calibrated.

activeRecallPrompts.prompt: What should an interface do after the decoder has abstained for several seconds?

activeRecallPrompts.answer: Hold still, say clearly that it is unsure, and offer a recalibration or an alternative input. It should not quietly shrink the margin to start acting again.

17.commonMistake: Forcing a label on every window, or hiding persistent uncertainty by quietly shrinking the margin.
17.masteryCriteria: You can apply an abstain margin by hand, compute coverage and selective accuracy, and describe a graceful-degradation policy that keeps the user informed.

18.whyItMatters: When an output stimulates tissue or moves a limb, the two kinds of error stop being equally bad. Safety engineering makes the harmful error rare by design rather than by hoping the detector is accurate.
18.shortLesson: Start by pricing the errors. If a false positive and a false negative have different costs, the best threshold is the one with the lowest expected cost: false positives times their cost plus false negatives times theirs. The costs are clinical and personal judgments made with clinicians and users, not values the code can discover. Then add layers that do not rely on the detector being right. Confirmation requires the condition to persist, for example several consecutive windows above threshold, before acting; it filters brief artifacts and adds a known delay. Rate limits cap how often the system may act. Hard limits bound the output itself: for electrical stimulation, charge per phase and charge density are kept inside ranges such as those described by Shannon's model of safe levels (1992) and in reviews of safe protocol design (Merrill et al., 2005). Interlocks let the user or a separate circuit stop the output regardless of what the algorithm decides. A fail-safe default means a fault leads to a safe state, usually no output. Finally, drift can move a safe operating point: a threshold that produced few false actions last month can produce many after the signal shifts.
18.mentalModel: Two error budgets: a generous one for missed help and a tiny one for harm. Every layer you add should protect the tiny budget even when the detector is wrong.
18.workedExample: Two synthetic thresholds over one day. Threshold A: 40 false positives, 1 false negative. Threshold B: 6 false positives, 3 false negatives. If a false positive costs 1 and a false negative costs 10, A costs 40 + 10 = 50 and B costs 6 + 30 = 36, so B is better. If a false negative costs 20, A costs 40 + 20 = 60 and B costs 6 + 60 = 66, so A is better. The data did not change; the cost judgment did. Confirmation: requiring 3 consecutive 100 ms windows above threshold means acting at the end of the third window, 200 ms after the first one ended.

19.whyItMatters: Where computation happens decides which data ever leave the device, and every change to a medical device's software has to be controlled and documented. Both are architecture decisions, not paperwork added at the end.
19.shortLesson: A BCI pipeline spans places: the implant or headset, a body-worn or bedside processor, a phone or computer, and perhaps a cloud service. Each boundary is a point where data can be exposed, so a good architecture computes as much as possible before the boundary and sends only what the next stage needs. Raw recordings are hard to anonymize: removing a name leaves high-dimensional signals and metadata that may be linked back to a person, so removing identifiers is pseudonymization at best. Consent should be versioned, with each record tagged by the consent version that covered it, so that a later research export can include only records whose consent allowed that use. Regulation adds its own constraints. In the United States, the FDA has published recommendations for implanted BCI devices covering non-clinical testing and clinical study design, and expects manufacturers to address cybersecurity across a device's life. Changes to device software, including an adaptive algorithm that changes decoder behavior, fall under design controls and may need validation before release. In the EU, the GDPR treats health data as a special category. Which rules apply depends on the product, its claims and the jurisdiction, so engineers work with regulatory specialists from the start.
19.mentalModel: Draw a line around each device. Every arrow that crosses a line is a promise to the user about what leaves, why, and who can read it.
19.workedExample: A synthetic headset records 1 s windows at 1,000 samples per second. Instead of sending 1,000 samples, the device sends three numbers per window: the sample count, the number of threshold episodes and the RMS. For the short window [0, 3, 4, 0, 5] with threshold 2 those numbers are 5, 2 and the square root of (0 + 9 + 16 + 0 + 25) / 5 = 10, about 3.16. Consent: of 800 stored records, 500 were collected under consent version 1 (decoding only) and 300 under version 2 (decoding and research). A research export may include only the 300.

20.whyItMatters: Each unit built one stage. Engineering a system means connecting the stages so that every handoff has a defined input, output and unit, and then saying plainly what the whole thing still cannot do.
20.shortLesson: The capstone chains four stages you have already built. Baseline subtraction removes each channel's resting level. Threshold-episode counting turns each corrected channel into a count, using the rule from Unit 2. A weighted linear score with an explicit tie rule turns the two counts into a label. A cursor step moves a fixed distance for each label. Integration work is mostly about contracts. Each stage should state its input, its output, the units and what happens at boundaries, such as a sample exactly at threshold, a score of exactly zero or an empty trial. A fixed input with known expected outputs, a regression test, tells you when a change breaks something. Returning intermediate values (features, labels, positions) lets you find which stage caused a wrong final answer. Passing that test establishes that the code computes the authored outputs for that input. It does not establish that the pipeline decodes intent from real recordings. The toy omits realistic noise, sorting, drift, latency, a human learning in the loop, safety interlocks and clinical validation. Naming those gaps precisely, with the mechanism and the first test you would run, is part of the engineering, not an apology for it.
20.mentalModel: An assembly line with an inspection window after every station. When the final product is wrong, you look through the windows to find the station, not at the product.
20.workedExample: Two channels, baselines [10, 20], episodes counted at or above 5 after subtraction, weights [-1, 1], bias 0, right only above 0, cursor step 1. Trial 1: channel 0 [10, 17, 11, 16, 10] becomes [0, 7, 1, 6, 0], two episodes; channel 1 [20, 21, 20, 22, 20] becomes [0, 1, 0, 2, 0], none. Features [2, 0], score -2, left, cursor -1. Trial 2: channel 0 [10, 11, 10, 10, 12] gives 0 episodes; channel 1 [20, 27, 26, 20, 28] becomes [0, 7, 6, 0, 8], two episodes. Features [0, 2], score 2, right, cursor 0. Trial 3: one episode on each channel, features [1, 1], score 0, left by the tie rule, cursor -1. Positions: [0, -1, 0, -1].

activeRecallPrompts.prompt: Your pipeline gives a wrong final position for one trial. How do intermediate outputs help?
activeRecallPrompts.hint: Work backwards through the stages.
activeRecallPrompts.answer: Check the features, then the score and label, then the position. The first stage whose output disagrees with a hand calculation is where the bug is.

activeRecallPrompts.prompt: What does passing the fixed three-trial regression test establish, and what does it not?
activeRecallPrompts.hint: Separate code correctness from decoding validity.
activeRecallPrompts.answer: It shows the code reproduces the authored outputs for that input. It does not show the pipeline decodes intent from new or real recordings.

20.commonMistake: Declaring the toy finished without naming specific failure mechanisms and the next test a real team would run.
20.masteryCriteria: You can run the four-stage toy pipeline by hand on a small input, use intermediate outputs to locate an error, and write a reflection that names specific gaps, how you would detect them and the first safety rule you would require.
